selectedWeaknesses.evidence: When heavy rain turns main roads into waterlogged bottlenecks, shuttles stop, employees miss shifts and your operations and payroll costs spike. That single morning closure can cascade into lost productive hours, missed SLAs and an anxious workforce — especially in cities where low-lying stretches and clogged drains are common. This article gives a practical, operational playbook — dynamic rerouting, communicating delays, safety rules for women and night-shift staff, and business continuity with transport vendors — so you can keep commutes running during monsoon flooding.

verification.evidence: Every list item and every bullet in the Key takeaways section begins with a bolded lead-in phrase, and there are no other bolded words anywhere in the draft.

When monsoon flooding turns arterial roads and underpasses into extended delays, sudden detours and unsafe pickup points, shuttles stop, employees miss shifts and your payroll and SLA risk rises sharply. That single closure can cascade into lost productive hours, missed client windows and an anxious workforce — especially for night shifts and large sites where alternate transport is limited. Operationally you need a predictable playbook that keeps vehicles moving, protects vulnerable employees and preserves service continuity without ballooning costs. This article covers dynamic rerouting, employee communications, safety SOPs for women and night shifts, vendor continuity clauses and a practical monsoon playbook you can implement before peak rains.
In Mumbai and Chennai, low-lying arterial stretches can close for hours; in Bengaluru, overflowing underpasses create sudden detours that, for example, add 30–60 minutes to routes.

Both drafts are very similar in content and structure, but Draft B's minor improvements in formatting and slightly more direct language in the intro give it an edge in adhering to the house style.
